key_insight: A personalised “digital twin” baseline can reveal hidden cardiac shape-and-function patterns that conventional measures like ejection fraction may miss.
clinical_relevance: These deviation phenotypes improved prediction of future cardiovascular events, especially atrial fibrillation in people with preserved ejection fraction, suggesting a path toward more precise risk stratification.
method: Built normative cardiac twins using age, sex, and body habitus to define expected healthy heart shape/function.
Compared individuals against two independent shape representations: HeartSSM (statistical shape model) and MeshHeart cVAE (deep latent mesh model).
Derived deviation scores and tested whether they added prognostic value beyond standard biomarkers, with placebo-noise controls and external validation.
evidence_signal: In UK Biobank cohorts, deviation scores improved risk prediction beyond standard biomarkers, with the strongest signal for incident atrial fibrillation in preserved-EF participants (ΔC up to +0.068; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3×10^-8) and a smaller independent signal for stroke in the alternate representation.
watch_item: The approach relies on specific imaging pipelines and shape representations, so broader clinical deployment will need robust standardisation and validation across scanners and populations.
paper_title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
